niche.title: Why Are Battleship Turrets Stacked on Top of Each Other?
niche.description:
Why are battleship turrets stacked on top of each other? 🔱

It is called superfiring — one turret raised behind the other so it can fire right over the top. Early dreadnoughts wasted guns in wing turrets that could not fire across the deck, so HMS Dreadnought needed ten guns for an eight-gun broadside. USS South Carolina put all eight of her twelve-inch guns on the centerline instead — and in 1907 the Navy proved it safe by firing over a manned turret on USS Florida.

niche.title: Why Old Ship Cannons Rolled Back After Firing
niche.description:
A broadside cannon on an old warship wasn't bolted down. Most people think a warship's cannon was bolted tight to the deck. Instead, it sat on a wooden carriage with small wheels, held by a thick breeching rope tied to the hull. When it fired, the whole gun rolled backward until that rope snapped tight and stopped it. But a gun bolted to the deck would slam its full kick into the timbers and crack them. Rolling back brought the muzzle inside the ship, where the crew could swab and reload it. Then the crew hauled it back out through the gun port with ropes and pulleys.

niche.title: Can a Tiger I Fire a Tiger II Shell?
niche.description:
Could the Tiger I use ammunition from the Tiger II?

Both German heavy tanks were armed with 88mm guns, but their ammunition was not interchangeable.

The Tiger I used the 8.8 cm KwK 36 L/56 with a 571mm cartridge case, while the Tiger II used the more powerful 8.8 cm KwK 43 L/71 with a longer 822mm case.

The Tiger II's larger cartridge could not fully fit inside the Tiger I's gun chamber.

This 3D animation demonstrates why two tanks with the same gun caliber required different ammunition.

The M1 Abrams is a powerful American main battle tank armed with a 120mm smoothbore cannon.

This helps reduce loose debris inside the cramped turret, where the crew operates the gun and handles ammunition. The design supports safer, more efficient operation in a confined space.

outliers.title: Why Are Battleship Turrets Stacked on Top of Each Other?
outliers.description:
Why are battleship turrets stacked on top of each other? 🔱

It is called superfiring — one turret raised behind the other so it can fire right over the top. Early dreadnoughts wasted guns in wing turrets that could not fire across the deck, so HMS Dreadnought needed ten guns for an eight-gun broadside. USS South Carolina put all eight of her twelve-inch guns on the centerline instead — and in 1907 the Navy proved it safe by firing over a manned turret on USS Florida.

outliers.title: Can a Tiger I Fire a Tiger II Shell?
outliers.description:
Could the Tiger I use ammunition from the Tiger II?

Both German heavy tanks were armed with 88mm guns, but their ammunition was not interchangeable.

The Tiger I used the 8.8 cm KwK 36 L/56 with a 571mm cartridge case, while the Tiger II used the more powerful 8.8 cm KwK 43 L/71 with a longer 822mm case.

The Tiger II's larger cartridge could not fully fit inside the Tiger I's gun chamber.

This 3D animation demonstrates why two tanks with the same gun caliber required different ammunition.

outliers.title: Why Old Ship Cannons Rolled Back After Firing
outliers.description:
A broadside cannon on an old warship wasn't bolted down. Most people think a warship's cannon was bolted tight to the deck. Instead, it sat on a wooden carriage with small wheels, held by a thick breeching rope tied to the hull. When it fired, the whole gun rolled backward until that rope snapped tight and stopped it. But a gun bolted to the deck would slam its full kick into the timbers and crack them. Rolling back brought the muzzle inside the ship, where the crew could swab and reload it. Then the crew hauled it back out through the gun port with ropes and pulleys.

- Sources: Naval artille

outliers.title: Mk 13: The Cold War Warship Missile Launcher That Fired 40 Missiles! #shorts
outliers.description:
The Mk 13 Guided Missile Launching System was a powerful naval weapon used on warships during the Cold War. Known as the "One-Armed Bandit," this launcher could store up to 40 missiles in two rotating magazine rings beneath the deck.

Its automated mechanism selected missiles and lifted them onto a single rotating launch arm. It could fire Standard missiles for air defense and Harpoon missiles against enemy ships. This innovative design allowed warships to launch missiles rapidly without manually reloading each round.
